newsitem.title: USA: Oil refining, marketing come to oil companies' rescue.
newsitem.headline: Oil refining, marketing come to oil companies' rescue.

text.p: More oil companies paraded earnings Wednesday that beat Wall Street's expectations as better refining and chemicals results offset the drag from lower oil prices.

All of the nation's top six oil companies have beaten earnings expectations this week, but the outlook for the industry is not rosy since there no promise of straight line growth in profits, analysts said.
Mobil Corp., USX-Marathon Group and Chevron Corp. all illustrated the benefits of having refining and marketing operations as a natural hedge against declining oil prices.
For the rest of the year, analysts say that the improving trend of refining earnings is set to continue, but perhaps at a slower rate.

"This is going to remain a cyclical business. While there is good gasoline demand, there is no shortage of capacity and the jump we saw this quarter will not be repeated," said Eugene Nowak, an analyst at ABN AMRO First Chicago Corp.

Mobil, the second-largest U.S. oil company, reported net income of $805 million, or $1.06 per share, including a $20 million charge due to the start-up of its European venture with British Petroleum Co. Plc. The income compared with profits of $783 million a year ago, or 98 cents a share.
The company said that refining and marketing income rose to $420 million from $352 million, although that rise was dampened by plant shutdowns in Asia.

This more than offset lower crude oil prices, which dropped by an average of 94 cents to $16.18 per barrel in the United States in the second quarter from the year-ago period. Prices tumbled $2.16 internationally over the same period.

Income from operations, which reveals the true state of the business, rose 7 percent to $870 million and earnings per share from operations were $1.09, vs. analysts' forecasts of $1.01 and an actual profits of $1.02 a year ago.
"Mobil's numbers were very good, but they were not the blowout that Exxon Corp. had on Monday and the shares had risen in anticipation of higher earnings," said Nowak.
Exxon, the largest U.S. oil company, reported a 25 percent jump in income.
Like Exxon, Mobil also saw an improved performance at its chemicals division, where income rose $26 million at $91 million.
USX-Marathon, the sixth-largest U.S. oil company, offset a 16 percent drop in oil and natural gas earnings with a bumper 31 percent rise in refining and marketing earnings to $165 million.

Its net income fell to $118 million from $124 million a year ago. But stripping out special items, income slid to $158 million, or 55 cents a share, from $169 million, or 59 cents a share, which was well above Wall Street's forecasts of 48 cents a share.
Chevron Corp. posted record operating earnings, up 20 percent at $700 million, despite a drop in sales to $9.95 billion from $10.51 billion.
Net income fell to $823 million, or $1.26 a share, from $872 million, or $1.34 per share, beating analysts' expectations of $1.10 per share.

The dangers of an oil company's dependency on drilling oil and natural gas alone without the benefit of a refining and marketing hedge was illustrated by Unocal Corp., where operating income per share of 39 cents, sharply below analysts' forecasts of 45 cents a share.

Unocal was fully exposed to a 7 percent fall in oil prices and its income was almost half the level of a year earlier at $118 million, or 48 cents per share, vs. $238 million, or 92 cents a share in the 1996 second quarter.
Mobil's stock fell $2 to $73.50, USX-Marathon rose 25 cents to $30.50, Chevron slid 81 cents to $76.94 and Unocal edged down 37.5 cents to $38.56, all on the New York Stock Exchange.
